description: We are developing an intuitive decision-support tool that leverages NASA Earth observations (SMAP, ECOSTRESS, GPM, Landsat) to recommend climate-resilient crop rotation strategies. Our platform analyzes soil moisture, heat stress, and rainfall patterns alongside local crop profiles to improve soil health and water conservation. Our team brings strong expertise in geospatial data analysis, satellite imagery processing, predictive modeling, and interactive web/GIS interface design.
summary:
SoilSight is an explainable farm-planning dashboard that transforms NASA Earth data into practical climate-adaptation guidance. A farmer draws a field on an interactive map, and SoilSight uses its centre point to retrieve NASA POWER temperature, precipitation, and land-surface wetness data. It then identifies risky months, estimates crop-water gaps, and compares three crop-rotation strategies: the farmer’s current rotation, a Soil-first plan, and a Water-saver plan.

Farmers can adjust priorities such as water conservation, soil health, market potential, and risk reduction. Every ranking includes plain-language explanations, assumptions, and confidence labels. A climate stress simulator also shows how the same plans could respond to hotter or drier conditions.

SoilSight addresses the challenge by converting complex NASA datasets into transparent, locally relevant planning insights. It is important because farmers need accessible tools to explore climate risk before making seasonal planting and water-management decisions.
details:
SoilSight begins with the farmer rather than the dataset. The user searches for a location and draws one farm or managed field using an interactive Leaflet map. The application calculates the field’s area and centre point, then requests regional climate information for that location from NASA POWER.

The dashboard presents monthly minimum, maximum, and average temperature, corrected precipitation, and root-zone and profile wetness. It clearly labels NASA POWER information as modelled regional data not field-sensor measurements or a weather forecast. NASA MODIS imagery provided through NASA GIBS is also available as a contextual map layer.

SoilSight converts these scientific inputs into several practical tools:

  • A 12-month risk calendar identifies periods of heat, cold, water deficit, or excess rainfall.
  • A smart irrigation planner estimates monthly crop-water need, effective rainfall, and supplemental water gaps.
  • A crop-planning engine evaluates crops across all 12 possible planting months.
  • Three strategies compare the farmer’s current rotation with Soil-first and Water-saver alternatives.
  • Priority sliders allow farmers to emphasize water conservation, soil health, nitrogen fixing, market potential, erosion control, or risk reduction.
  • A climate stress simulator recalculates the same plans under hypothetical temperature and rainfall changes.
  • Historical NASA POWER analysis shows rainfall and temperature trends and unusually wet or dry years.
  • A template-based field advisor and action plan translate the results into understandable next steps.

The recommendations are produced by a transparent rules-based engine rather than a black-box model. Crop suitability combines seasonal temperature fit, rainfall adequacy, irrigation demand, and estimated soil compatibility. The interface explains why each strategy received its score, identifies missing evidence, and always recommends review by a local agronomist. Soil estimates are treated as provisional, and the application safely uses a neutral contribution when a reliable local soil profile is unavailable.

We developed SoilSight using React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, Leaflet, Leaflet Draw, Recharts, Node.js, and Vercel serverless functions. Vitest tests the calculations, while Playwright and axe-core test complete user journeys, responsive behavior, and accessibility. The application requires no special hardware and can run through a modern web browser on desktop or mobile devices.

SoilSight is creative because it does more than visualize NASA data: it creates an explainable decision pipeline from field selection to adaptation planning. The team considered data resolution, unreliable external services, regional neutrality, accessibility, multilingual support, scientific uncertainty, and the danger of presenting estimates as facts. Every result is labelled as modelled, estimated, imported, or demonstrational so users understand both its value and its limitations.

The intended impact is to help farmers, advisors, and agricultural organizations begin better evidence-based conversations about crop choice, seasonal risk, irrigation demand, and climate resilience while keeping local knowledge and expert review at the centre of the final decision.
